message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) Below is a concise guide to your key rights as a renter in Texas. These rights apply to most residential leases, but always check your lease agreement and local ordinances for specifics. | Category | Your Rights | |----------|-------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Texas law caps the amount at **two months’ rent** for unfurnished units and **three months’ rent** for furnished units.
• Landlords must return the deposit within **30 days** after you move out, unless they provide a written itemized list of deductions. | | **Habitability** | • Your landlord must keep the property in a safe, livable condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc.
• If repairs are needed, you can request them in writing; if the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (subject to court approval). | | **Rent Payment** | • You’re required to pay rent on time per the lease. Late fees are allowed only if specified in the lease and must be reasonable. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month rentals: **30 days’ written notice** from either party to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: the lease ends automatically unless renewed or extended. | | **Eviction Process** | • A landlord must serve a **notice** (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 10‑day notice for lease violations).
• After the notice period, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action in court. You’ll receive a summons and have a chance to respond. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering your unit, except in emergencies. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | | **Lease Modifications** | • Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | | **Right to Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair them yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow proper procedures and obtain court approval. | | **Legal Assistance** | • If you face disputes, consider contacting:
– Texas Attorney General’s Office (Consumer Protection Division)
– Local legal aid organizations
– Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs | --- #### Quick Steps If You Encounter Problems 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, photos of issues, and receipts for repairs. 2. **Send Written Notice** – Notify your landlord in writing of any problem and request repairs. 3. **Follow Up** – If the landlord doesn’t act, send a second notice or consider withholding rent (only after consulting a lawyer). 4. **Seek Mediation** – Many counties offer free mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 5. **File a Complaint** – If necessary, file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s office or pursue a lawsuit in small claims court. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on tenant rights, filing complaints, and consumer protection. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs** | Guidance on fair housing, rental assistance, and housing codes. | | **Local Legal Aid Societies** | Free or low‑cost legal advice for tenants. | | **Small Claims Court** | A venue to resolve disputes involving amounts up to $20,000. | --- **Note:** Laws can change, and local ordinances may add extra protections. Always verify current regulations and consult a qualified attorney if you’re facing a serious issue.
